studyPages.body:
WHY MATERIALS MOVE IN CELLS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what why materials move in cells means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show why materials move in cells.
• Correct one common mistake about why materials move in cells.

INTRODUCTION
----
Quick question: how would you explain Why Materials Move in Cells — Need for uptake and removal to a classmate in one minute? Anchor answer: Need for uptake and removal. Clue from real life: 2.2 Movement of Material in and Out of the Cell. Check every example on this page against that anchor.

MAIN NOTES
----
• 2.2 Movement of Material in and Out of the Cell.
• Diffusion is defined as the movement of molecules from a region of high concentratio to a region of low concentratio.
• Cells and unicellular organisms such as amoeba get rid of waste substance through diffusion.
• Gaseous exchange is the process through which gases are transferred across cell membrane to either enter or leave the blood. This process is done by diffusion in human beings in the alveoli in lungs. Oxygen gas moves from alveoli where is it is highly concentrated to the blood capillaries where it is lowly concentrated.
• Temperature-high temperature increases energy and therefore faster movement of molecules. This increases the rate of diffusion.
• What can we compare the visking tubing with in living cells?.
• Osmosis is the random movement of water (solvent) molecules from there they are more to where they are less through a semi-permeable membrane.

----
Worked situation (a hardware shop in Nakuru): a learner investigates why materials move in cells. First observation: 2.2 Movement of Material in and Out of the Cell. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a hardware shop in Nakuru, why materials move in cells shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Practical tip: compare two cases (right vs wrong) so the idea sticks for exams.

SOLUTES SOLVENTS AND SOLUTIONS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what solutes solvents and solutions means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show solutes solvents and solutions.
• Correct one common mistake about solutes solvents and solutions.

INTRODUCTION
----
Take one familiar object tied to solutes solvents and solutions. Watch this detail: When a solid is dissolved in a liquid, we get a solution formed. The science under it is Definitions with sugar/salt water. That is the whole job of this page: name it correctly and apply it.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A solute is the substance that dissolves, for example sugar or salt.
• A solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving. Water is the most common solvent in school experiments and in the body.
• A solution is the mixture formed when the solute dissolves completely in the solvent.
• A concentrated solution has a lot of solute compared with solvent. A dilute solution has little solute compared with solvent.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Tonny stirs three spoons of sugar into a glass of water at a kitchen in Kisumu. First name the parts: sugar is the solute, water is the solvent. Because the sugar disappears into the water, the sweet liquid is a solution. Next he makes a second glass with only half a spoon of sugar — that one is more dilute. Same solute and solvent; different amounts change the concentration.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a kitchen in Kisumu, solutes solvents and solutions shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: if you see smoke, raise the alarm early and do not fight a large fire alone.

SUMMARY
----
• A solute is the substance that dissolves, for example sugar or salt.
• A solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving. Water is the most common solvent in school experiments and in the body.
• A solution is the mixture formed when the solute dissolves completely in the solvent.
• A concentrated solution has a lot of solute compared with solvent. A dilute solution has little solute compared with solvent.

studyPages.title: Diffusion Defined
studyPages.body:
DIFFUSION DEFINED
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what diffusion defined means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show diffusion defined.
• Correct one common mistake about diffusion defined.

INTRODUCTION
----
Open a bottle of perfume in one corner of a classroom and soon learners at the far wall can smell it — even though nobody walked the scent across. Particles moved from where they were concentrated to where they were less concentrated. That net movement is diffusion.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
• It happens in gases and liquids without anyone stirring.
• Perfume opened in one corner of a classroom is soon smelled elsewhere because perfume particles diffuse through air.
• A drop of ink in still water spreads as ink particles diffuse through the water.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (a shamba in Nyeri): a learner investigates diffusion defined. First observation: Experiment demonstrating diffusion in gases. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a shamba in Nyeri, diffusion defined shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Practical tip: write the correct symbol or formula before you explain out loud.

SUMMARY
----
• Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
• It happens in gases and liquids without anyone stirring.
• Perfume opened in one corner of a classroom is soon smelled elsewhere because perfume particles diffuse through air.
• A drop of ink in still water spreads as ink particles diffuse through the water.

INTRODUCTION

Put a drop of the dye or ink in the water. That single observation is enough to unlock Diffusion in Liquids Experiment — Ink or dye in water. Also notice: After a few minutes, the ink or dye spread throughout the water in the beaker. Put simply, you are learning why that happens and how to say it accurately in an exam.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Put a drop of the dye or ink in the water.
• After a few minutes, the ink or dye spread throughout the water in the beaker.
• Concentratio gradient-molecules move from region of high concentratio to that of low concentratio. The greater the difference in concentratio between high and low regions, the faster the rate of diffusion.
• Mass of particles- heavy particles move slowly hence slower rate of diffusion. Light particles on the other hand move fast hence faster rate of diffusion.
• Diffusion distance- rate of diffusion depends on distance that particles have to travel in order to be evenly distributed within available space.
• Medium of diffusion- particles diffuse faster through gases than liquids.
• Surface area to volume ratio- diffusion occurs faster in smaller organisms as compared to larger organisms. This is because small organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio.

studyPages.title: Osmosis Defined
studyPages.body:
OSMOSIS DEFINED
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what osmosis defined means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show osmosis defined.
• Correct one common mistake about osmosis defined.

INTRODUCTION
----
Soak dry beans overnight and they swell as water enters. Water crossed into the beans through tiny openings toward the more concentrated cell contents. Osmosis is that special case: water moving across a selectively permeable membrane.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution toward a more concentrated solution.
• The membrane lets water pass more easily than large solute particles.
• Visking tubing filled with sugar solution and placed in distilled water gains water by osmosis — a school model of the process.
• Living cells use osmosis to take in or lose water depending on the surrounding solution.
